S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder is characterized by intrusive, unwanted obsessions and repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent feared outcomes, with the cycle becoming time-consuming or functionally impairing. Its course is often gradual and fluctuating, and it is distinguished from ordinary worry, perfectionism, or safety-conscious habits by the intrusive quality of the thoughts and the excessive, rigid nature of the compulsive responses.

patient.stressor: After Darnell sustained a wrist fracture in a fall on the way home from a gallery event, his recovery temporarily narrowed his world to medical appointments, home routines, and a slower pace of reading, gardening, and volunteer work. During that period, intrusive unwanted concerns about contamination, harm, and whether he had completed small daily tasks began to attach themselves to ordinary activities that had previously felt calming. He started relying on repetitive behaviors and mental checking that were excessive for the situation, causing him to arrive late to docent shifts and avoid some museum outings, though he remained largely independent. When he mentioned during a follow-up visit that these routines were becoming harder to interrupt than the wrist pain itself, his primary care clinician referred him for psychiatric assessment.

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: I’ll be reading at home or getting ready for a museum shift, and an ugly little thought keeps barging in that I’ve left something unsafe, touched something unclean, or somehow put someone at risk, even though I know perfectly well it’s out of proportion.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: What brings me in is that I’ve gotten stuck doing these little routines—washing my hands again after handling my wrist brace, rechecking the stove and front door, silently counting through steps before I leave—and they’re starting to make me late even when I know I’ve already done enough.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: I’m still managing on my own, but these routines have made me late to docent shifts and have led me to skip a few museum events because getting out the door feels like too much.
